title: Festivals and everyday culture
job: Talk about what is happening around you
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: -deon IS THE RETROSPECTIVE MODIFIER, the fourth this course opens. halmeoni-ga mandeuldeon tteokguk is the tteokguk grandmother used to make — a thing done over and over and now remembered as such. It carries a feeling as well as a tense, which none of L3-M2's three does.

-eoss-eoss- IS THE DOUBLE PAST, and it means used to and does not any more. yejeon-e-neun jaju gasseosseoyo says the going is over, which the plain gasseoyo does not. Both frames arrive here as ONE frame each; neither paradigm is opened.

THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THEM IS WHAT THEY ATTACH TO, NOT WHAT THEY MEAN. English splits used to across a modifier and a verb ending too — the food she used to make, I used to go — and Korean does the same with -deon in front of a noun and -eoss-eoss- at the end of a clause.

L2-M7's -go isseoyo gets its second life and nothing is opened for it: saram-deul-i sajin-eul jjikgo isseoyo is what a crowd is doing at this moment, which is the reading L2-M7 reserved it for. L2-M9's -eun/-neun does the then-against-now contrast, also unchanged.

L2-M3's -deul finally has a sentence that needs it. Number is optional in Korean rather than absent, and a crowd is where it stops being optional: saram-deul-i is people as a group you can see, where bare saram would leave the sentence oddly singular.

A FESTIVAL IS PLACED WITH -e AND NEVER WITH A CLAUSE. Seollal-e tteokguk-eul meogeoyo. English reaches for when it is Seollal, and every time clause in this course — -(eu)l ttae and its family — is L4-M6's. ttae is not written anywhere in this module.

THE CLAIMS STAY SMALL. A display says what is on the street; usage says when the day falls and who does what. Korea is not one custom, and nothing here is asserted as universal — an author reaching for colour is how a course starts lecturing.

The festival names take rows of their own, as hanguk, kim, minsu and yuna already do on this course. A proper noun with no row is a word shown and not taught, and the ratchet counts it; giving it a row costs one key and keeps the module honest.

words.note: The autumn festival, on the fifteenth of the eighth lunar month, so it moves in the solar calendar. Families travel to where they are from.
The class word Seollal and Chuseok both belong to — a holiday with customs attached, as against hyuil, which is only a day off.
A day nobody works, with nothing traditional about it. Every myeongjeol is a hyuil; most hyuil are not myeongjeol.

sentences.trap: -eun IS DOING REAL WORK HERE. It sets today against the ordinary days around it, which is exactly what an announcement wants; -i would make today the plain subject and the sentence flat.
sentences.sound: O-neu-reun CHU-seo-gi-e-yo. Chuseok-ieyo runs together as CHU-seo-gi-e-yo.

variations.cue: Today is a traditional holiday.
variations.changed: the class word in place of the festival's own name

variations.cue: Tomorrow is a day off.
variations.changed: L1-M6's naeil, and a day with no customs attached to it

mistake.why: That answers which day is Chuseok. To announce the day, Oneul-eun Chuseok-ieyo.

sentences.usage: Explaining why the streets are empty or the shops are shut.
sentences.mnemonic: myeongjeol has customs, hyuil has none.

words.note: L1-M1's saram with L2-M3's -deul. Number is optional in Korean, and a crowd is the case where leaving it off would read oddly singular.
The picture itself. Taking one is jjikda, a verb that also does stamping and pressing, so it is the pressing of the shutter.
L1-M10's -go, and L2-M7's -go isseoyo is what makes it right now. The jj is tense: no puff of air on it at all.

sentences.trap: -go isseoyo IS NOT THE DEFAULT PRESENT. L1-M4's plain -yo already covers what usually happens; this form is for what is visibly under way in front of you, which is why a crowd is where it belongs.
sentences.sound: SA-ram-deu-ri SA-ji-neul JJIK-go I-sseo-yo. saram-deul-i is SA-ram-deu-ri.

variations.cue: People are eating tteokguk.
variations.changed: L1-M4's meokda in the same progressive frame

variations.cue: My friends are taking photos.
variations.changed: L2-M3's chingu-deul, a group you can name rather than a crowd

mistake.why: That is one person. For the crowd it is Saram-deul-i sajin-eul jjikgo isseoyo.

sentences.usage: Describing a square, a parade or a market as you stand in it.
sentences.mnemonic: -go isseoyo is what you can see.

words.note: Lunar new year, so it moves against the solar calendar. Spelled seol-nal and said seol-lal, which is what the romanization writes.
Sliced rice cake in a clear broth, eaten at Seollal. The tt is tense, and the word is two nouns pushed together: rice cake and soup.
Half-moon rice cakes with a sweet filling, steamed over pine needles and made at Chuseok, where tteokguk belongs to Seollal.

sentences.trap: NOBODY IS NAMED AND THAT IS THE POINT. With no subject the sentence says what is done rather than what any one person does, which is how a custom is stated; adding jeo-neun would turn it into an autobiography.
sentences.sound: SEOL-la-re TTEOK-gu-geul MEO-geo-yo. seol-nal is said SEOL-lal — the n has become a second l.

variations.cue: People eat songpyeon at Chuseok.
variations.changed: the other festival with the food that belongs to it

variations.cue: Seollal is a traditional holiday.
variations.changed: the festival as the topic rather than as the date

mistake.why: -eseo is for a place where something happens; a day takes -e. Seollal-e tteokguk-eul meogeoyo.

sentences.usage: Answering what people do on the day, when somebody asks.

sentences.cue: The tteokguk my grandmother used to make is delicious.

words.note: Your own and anybody's, and the polite way to address an older woman you do not know. L1-M7's family words gain their oldest generation here.
L3-M8's mandeureoyo with -deon on it. The ending remembers: it says the making happened again and again and belongs to the past.

sentences.trap: -deon IS NOT L3-M2's -(eu)n. mandeun tteokguk is the tteokguk she made, once; mandeuldeon tteokguk is the one she used to make, and only the second carries the looking back.
sentences.sound: HAL-meo-ni-ga MAN-deul-deon TTEOK-gu-gi MA-si-sseo-yo. tteokguk-i is TTEOK-gu-gi.

variations.cue: The songpyeon my grandmother used to make is delicious.
variations.changed: the other festival food under the same remembered clause

variations.cue: The restaurant I used to go to is good.
variations.changed: -deon on L1-M4's gada, with L1-M6's sikdang as the head noun

mistake.why: The clause goes in front of its noun, as L3-M2 taught: Halmeoni-ga mandeuldeon tteokguk-i masisseoyo.

sentences.usage: Talking about food, and about the person it came from.

words.note: A vague earlier time, years rather than days. Two particles stack on it: -e places it, and -neun sets it against now.

words.cue: used to go (and no longer do)
words.note: L1-M5's gasseoyo with a second past inside it. The extra -eoss- cuts the going off from now, which the plain past does not.

sentences.trap: TWO PASTS DO NOT MEAN LONGER AGO. gasseosseoyo is not a pluperfect; it says the habit has ended, so it answers do you still go rather than when did you go.
sentences.sound: YE-jeo-ne-neun JA-ju GA-sseo-sseo-yo. The two sseo syllables are both tense and both said in full.

variations.cue: I used to do it often.
variations.changed: the same double past on L1-M4's hada

variations.cue: People wore hanbok in the old days.
variations.changed: the plain past, which reports the fact without saying the habit has stopped

mistake.why: yejeon-e-neun has already put the sentence in the past, so the verb cannot stay in the present: Yejeon-e-neun jaju gasseosseoyo.

sentences.usage: Saying what you gave up, without being asked why.
sentences.mnemonic: Two pasts, and it is over.

words.note: L2-M7's jigeum with L1-M1's -eun on it. The particle is the whole point: it answers yejeon-e-neun and makes one sentence out of two times.
Different from what came before, with the comparison left to the sentence around it. It is a descriptive verb, so no copula follows it.

sentences.trap: THE PAIR IS THE POINT, NOT THE WORDS. yejeon-e-neun … jigeum-eun … is L2-M9's contrast doing its second job, and either half alone is a plain statement rather than a comparison.
sentences.sound: JI-geu-meun MYEONG-jeo-ri DAL-la-yo. The ll of dallayo is long and held.

variations.cue: I used to go often. Now it's different.
variations.changed: the two halves said together, which is how the contrast is actually used

variations.cue: It's a holiday now.
variations.changed: the same topic marker in front of a plain statement

mistake.why: Without -eun there is nothing for now to stand against. Jigeum-eun myeongjeol-i dallayo.

sentences.usage: The second half of any then-and-now remark.

sentences.cue: There are a lot of people wearing hanbok.

words.note: Worn at festivals, at weddings and for photographs, and hired by the hour near a palace. han is the same syllable as in hanguk.
L3-M2's past modifier, but the English is a present: the putting on is finished and the clothes are still on. ipgo isseoyo is the act of dressing.

sentences.trap: THE PAST MODIFIER GIVES A PRESENT MEANING. ipeun saram is a person wearing it now, because Korean marks the putting-on as done; a learner who writes ipneun saram has described somebody getting dressed.
sentences.sound: HAN-bo-geul I-peun SA-ram-deu-ri MA-na-yo. hanbok-eul is HAN-bo-geul.

variations.cue: People wear hanbok at Chuseok.
variations.changed: the plain verb, so the clause disappears and the custom is stated

variations.display: Hanbok-eul ipeun saram-deul-i sajin-eul jjikgo isseoyo.
variations.script: 한복을 입은 사람들이 사진을 찍고 있어요.
variations.cue: People in hanbok are taking photos.
variations.changed: the clause and the progressive in one sentence, which is the whole module

mistake.why: The clause has to sit in front of the noun it describes: Hanbok-eul ipeun saram-deul-i manayo.

sentences.usage: Describing a scene at a palace, a festival or a wedding.

sentences.cue: People bow to their elders at Seollal.

words.cue: sebae — the new year bow to an elder
words.note: The deep bow made to elders at Seollal, usually answered with a word of blessing and often with money. It is a noun, and haeyo is what does it.
A day thought of by what happens on it, so it almost always has a clause in front: sebaehaneun nal, the day people do sebae.

sentences.trap: THE CUSTOM IS A NOUN PLUS haeyo. Korean names the act and then does it, so there is no single verb to look up; the same shape gives gongbuhaeyo and jeonhwahaeyo, both L1's.
sentences.sound: SEOL-la-re SE-bae-reul HAE-yo. sebae is two syllables, se and bae, evenly stressed.

variations.cue: It's the day people do sebae.
variations.changed: L3-M2's present modifier naming the day by what happens on it

variations.cue: People don't do sebae at Chuseok.
variations.changed: L1-M3's an, and the custom pinned to one festival rather than to both

mistake.why: The bow is what is done, so it takes the object particle: Seollal-e sebae-reul haeyo.

sentences.usage: Explaining the morning of new year to somebody who has not seen it.

words.note: Whose birthday it is comes from the conversation, not from the sentence; saeng is birth and il is the Sino day, written only inside the word.
Anything given, at a birthday or on a first visit to somebody's home. It is received with L2-M3's badayo, never with a verb of taking.

sentences.trap: NOTHING SAYS WHOSE. Korean leaves the owner out once the situation supplies it, so je saengil is only said when the point is that it is yours and not somebody else's.
sentences.sound: O-neu-reun SAENG-i-ri-e-yo. saengil is SAENG-il, with no extra n between the syllables.

variations.cue: My friend bought a present.
variations.changed: L1-M8's sada in the past, with the gift as its object

variations.cue: People get presents on their birthday.
variations.changed: the day placed with -e, exactly as a festival is

mistake.why: The sentence still needs its copula: Oneul-eun saengil-ieyo.

sentences.usage: Saying why you are being taken out, or why the cake is there.

sentences.cue: There are a lot of people at the festival.

words.note: A public event with stalls and a stage — a town's spring fair, a university's week — and not a myeongjeol, which is a day in the calendar.

sentences.trap: chukje AND myeongjeol ARE NOT THE SAME WORD. A myeongjeol is a holiday families keep; a chukje is an event somebody organises, and calling Chuseok a chukje is heard as a mistake rather than as a loose usage.
sentences.sound: CHUK-je-e SA-ram-deu-ri MA-na-yo. The two e sounds of chukje-e are said as one long one.

variations.cue: There's a festival today.
variations.changed: L1-M7's isseoyo announcing the event rather than describing the crowd

variations.cue: I used to go to the festival.
variations.changed: the double past, saying the going belongs to earlier years

mistake.why: manayo says what is there rather than what happens, so the particle is -e: Chukje-e saram-deul-i manayo.

sentences.usage: Warning a friend what the evening will be like, or explaining the noise.
sentences.mnemonic: chukje is put on, myeongjeol comes round.

comprehensionPool.cue: The tteokguk my grandmother used to make is delicious.
There are a lot of people wearing hanbok.
People bow to their elders at Seollal.
There are a lot of people at the festival.
